Surface Areas
and Volumes

A water tanker is a cylinder with two hemispheres bolted on. A test tube is a cylinder with one. A lattu is a cone sitting on a hemisphere. Real objects are rarely one shape — they are two shapes glued together. This chapter is about measuring them without taking them apart.

6 solids1 rule for area1 rule for volume17 NCERT questions
SURFACE AREA: add only the surfaces you can still see.
VOLUME: just add everything, nothing disappears.
Drawing sheet 01

01The chapter in one drawing

Two ideas, and they behave completely differently when you join two solids.

RULE 1
Surface area: only what shows
When two faces are glued, both disappear. Subtract the hidden circles.
RULE 2
Volume: nothing disappears
Glue does not destroy material. Total volume = sum of volumes.
TOOL 1
Break it into basic solids
Cylinder, cone, sphere, hemisphere, cuboid, cube — nothing else is needed.
TOOL 2
Pythagoras for slant height
l = √(r² + h²) — the most-forgotten line in the paper.
Surface area: add the exposed faces
Volume: add everything

CSA vs TSA in one line CSA counts only the curved skin. TSA counts the curved skin plus every flat face. A cone has one flat face (the base); a hemisphere has one; a cylinder has two; a sphere has none.

The forgotten step

04Slant height: the number they hide from you

Questions love to give you the height of a cone and then ask for a surface area, which needs the slant height. The cone's cross-section is a right triangle: radius across, height up, slant along the side.

Interactive · Pythagoras at work

Most textbook triples are Pythagorean: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (7,24,25) and their multiples. If r = 3.5 and h = 12, then l = 12.5 — spot the 7-24-25 pattern.

Worked examples 1–4

05Surface area, worked properly

Example 1 · Rasheed's lattu (cone on hemisphere)

Height 5 cm, diameter 3.5 cm, π = 22/7. Find the area to colour.

Step-through · Example 1
The classic “find the hidden radius first” problem.
Radius. d = 3.5, so r = 1.75 cm. The hemisphere sits on top, so its radius is also the radius of the cone.
Height of the cone. Total 5 cm minus the hemisphere's height (its radius, 1.75) gives h = 3.25 cm.
Slant height. l = √(1.75² + 3.25²) = √(3.0625 + 10.5625) = √13.625 ≈ 3.7 cm.
CSA hemisphere = 2πr² = 2(22/7)(3.0625) = 19.25 cm².
CSA cone = πrl = (22/7)(1.75)(3.7) = 20.35 cm².
Total = 19.25 + 20.35 = 39.6 cm². Note: this is not the sum of the two total surface areas — the flat circles are glued and invisible.

Example 2 · The decorative block (cube + hemisphere)

Cube edge 5 cm, hemisphere diameter 4.2 cm, π = 22/7.

Step-through · Example 2
One face is lost, one circle is gained.
Cube TSA = 6a² = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².
Lose the covered circle. r = 2.1 cm, so πr² = 13.86 cm² disappears from the top face.
Gain the dome. CSA of hemisphere = 2πr² = 27.72 cm².
Net. 150 − 13.86 + 27.72 = 163.86 cm², i.e. 150 + πr².

Examples 3 & 4 · Rocket and bird-bath

l = √(2.5² + 6²) = 6.5 cm.

Orange = CSA cone + base of cone − base of cylinder = π(2.5×6.5) + π(2.5²) − π(1.5²) = π[16.25 + 6.25 − 2.25] = 3.14 × 20.25 = 63.585 cm².

Yellow = CSA cylinder + one base = 2π(1.5)(20) + π(2.25) = 188.4 + 7.065 = 195.465 cm².

The ring matters: the cone's base is wider than the cylinder, so an annulus stays visible.

TSA = CSA of cylinder + CSA of the hemispherical hollow = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r).

= 2(22/7)(30)(145 + 30) = 33000 cm² = 3.3 m².

The top is open, so no flat circle is counted; the depression adds a curved surface, not a flat one.

06Volume: the easy half

Glue cannot destroy material. So for volume there is no subtraction and no “hidden face” — just add the pieces. Watch the bar fill as the pieces stack.

Examples 5–7, solved

Volume = 15×7×8 + ½(22/7)(3.5²)(15) = 840 + 288.75 = 1128.75 m³.

Air = 1128.75 − (300 + 20×0.08) = 1128.75 − 301.6 = 827.15 m³.

Apparent = πr²h = 3.14(6.25)(10) = 196.25 cm³.

Hemisphere removed = (2/3)(3.14)(15.625) = 32.71 cm³.

Actual = 196.25 − 32.71 = 163.54 cm³.

r = 2. Toy = (2/3)π(8) + (1/3)π(4)(2) = 16.75 + 8.37 = 25.12 cm³.

Cylinder: r = 2, height = 2 + 2 = 4, volume = 3.14(4)(4) = 50.24 cm³.

Difference = 50.24 − 25.12 = 25.12 cm³ — half the cylinder, which is a pleasing check.

Marks lost here

09Five mistakes that repeat every year

01

Adding two TSAs

When faces are glued they vanish. Always list the surfaces that remain visible.

02

Using h instead of l

Cone surface area needs the slant height. Compute l = √(r² + h²) before anything else.

03

Forgetting the ring

When a wide cone sits on a narrow cylinder, an annulus of the cone's base stays visible.

04

Mixing units

1.45 m and 30 cm in the same question. Convert first: 145 cm and 30 cm.

05

Counting the base twice

A hemisphere on a cylinder loses one circle. A capsule (two hemispheres) loses two.

Doubts, answered

12Frequently asked questions

Because at the join, two faces are pressed together and neither is on the outside any more. Paint cannot reach them, so they are not part of the surface. Volume, on the other hand, is material — it simply adds.

Every glued joint removes two matching faces from the sum. For a hemisphere on a cylinder that is one circle from the hemisphere and one from the cylinder — so instead of TSA = (3πr²) + 2πr(h+r), you count only the visible parts. The safe method: sketch, then tick each visible surface.

CSA = 2πr² (the dome only). TSA = 3πr² (dome plus the flat circular base). A hemisphere used as a lid contributes only its CSA, because its flat face is glued down.

h is the perpendicular height (for volume), l is the slant height (for surface area). They are related by l² = r² + h². If a question gives the total height of a toy, subtract the hemisphere's radius to get the cone's own h.

Subtract the volume of the cavity. For surface area, the cavity's inner surface becomes visible and must be added, while the circle it was cut from disappears — the NCERT pen-stand and cylinder-cavity questions both follow this pattern.

Always, before calculating. Areas come out in cm² or m², volumes in cm³ or m³, and 1 m² = 10,000 cm², 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³, 1 litre = 1000 cm³. A mixed-unit question is the most common place to lose a mark in this chapter.

Exercise 12.1 · Surface areas

Edge = 4 cm → 8 × 4 × 4. TSA = 2(32 + 16 + 32) = 160 cm².

r = 7, cylinder h = 6. Inner SA = 2πr² + 2πrh = 308 + 264 = 572 cm².

l = 12.5. TSA = 2πr² + πrl = 77 + 137.5 = 214.5 cm².

Greatest diameter = 7 cm, r = 3.5.

SA = 6(49) − πr² + 2πr² = 294 + 38.5 = 332.5 cm².

SA = 6l² − π(l/2)² + 2π(l/2)² = 6l² + πl²/4 = l²(24 + π)/4.

With π = 22/7 this is (95/14)l².

r = 2.5, cylinder length 9. SA = 2πr² + 2πrh = 39.29 + 141.43 = 180.71 mm².

Area = 2π(2)(2.1) + π(2)(2.8) = 26.4 + 17.6 = 44 m²; cost = ₹22,000.

l = 2.5. TSA = 2πrh + πr² + πrl = 10.56 + 1.54 + 5.5 = 17.6 ≈ 18 cm².

TSA = 2πrh + 4πr² = 220 + 154 = 374 cm².

Chapter summary

15What you must be able to do

  • Break any combined object into basic solids: cuboid, cube, cylinder, cone, sphere, hemisphere
  • Find surface area by adding only the exposed surfaces — glued faces disappear
  • Find volume by simply adding the volumes of the parts
  • Use l = √(r² + h²) whenever a cone's slant height is needed
  • Subtract cavity volumes, and add cavity surfaces that become visible
Chapter 12 · Surface Areas and Volumes — built from the NCERT Class X textbook (Reprint 2026–27). List the visible faces, then add. That is the whole method.
